```bash

wc -l introduction.tex method.tex experiments.tex discussion.tex related_work.tex conclusion.tex appendix.tex
```

**务必逐一检查，哪些在 appendix 中需要拉回，哪些已在正文中无需改动。**

#### 2a. Cross-model 分析（→ experiments.tex）
这是 Claim 2（跨模型泛化）的核心证据。必须在 Experiments 正文中包含：
- Qwen vs DeepSeek 跨模型对比表（Table: cross_model）
- exception_only 跨模型 gap = 0.50pp (99.83% vs 99.33%)
- VOTA 跨模型 gap = 14.96pp (99.41% vs 84.45%)
- DeepSeek full_trace 79.16%
- DeepSeek no_trace 73.36%
- 简要讨论 truncation confound（2-3 句，详细分析仍在 Appendix）

```latex
\centering

\caption{Cross-model accuracy gap...}
\label{fig:cross_model_gap}
\end{figure}
```

4. Future Work（3-5 句：多语言、更大模型、更多数据集、production 部署）

```bash
grep "^!" main.log | head -5
```

- **所有数字必须与 registry 一致**

- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.

Verdict prediction is fundamentally a fault detection task: the model must determine whether execution deviated from expected behavior.
Exception events are the most explicit signal of such deviation---structured diagnostic moments that encode the nature and location of a fault.

\paragraph{Execution Traces for Code LLMs.}
Several recent efforts have incorporated execution traces into code language model training.
TracePile \citep{chen2025tracepile} scaled trace-augmented training to 2.6M samples across multiple programming languages, demonstrating gains on code generation tasks.
\citet{wang2025dcsh} conducted a comprehensive study of execution trace-based information for code LLMs across synthesis, repair, and reasoning tasks, finding that trace-based semantic information has limited and inconsistent utility---a finding our work extends by showing that for \emph{verdict prediction}, exception events are a clear dominant signal.

ET-CoT \citep{eguchi2025etcot} introduced sub-line granularity traces via PyTracify, achieving 70.0\% on CRUXEval-O with SFT on Qwen2.5-7B.
\citet{jung2025execution} used debugger-extracted traces as grounded supervision for LLM reasoning, reducing overthinking while improving cross-domain transfer.
\citet{ferrando2025execute} compared regular, compact, and dynamic scratchpad strategies, finding that compact traces (recording only changed variables) perform comparably to full traces---directly supporting our finding that complete value information is redundant.
CRUXEval \citep{gu2024cruxeval} established benchmarks for code execution reasoning; CRUXEval-X \citep{xu2025cruxevalx} extended this to 19 programming languages.
A common limitation across these studies is that they focus on generation or output prediction tasks; none have decomposed which trace components contribute to \emph{classification} accuracy or tested cross-model generalization of trace signals.

\paragraph{Code Verdict and Patch Classification.}
TRACED \citep{ding2024traced} showed that execution-aware pretraining improves vulnerability detection and clone detection, using encoder-based models with trace-augmented objectives.
In automated patch correctness prediction, APPT \citep{appt2024} fine-tuned pre-trained models with BERT+LSTM achieving 79.7\% accuracy on Defects4J patches, while LLM4PatchCorrect \citep{zhou2024llm4patch} used Starcoder-7B zero-shot with execution traces reaching 84.4\%.
More recently, \citet{yang2025apsg} proposed Graph-LoRA with attributed patch semantic graphs for parameter-efficient patch classification.
FuseFL \citep{widyasari2024fusefl} fused SBFL rankings with test execution outcomes (including error messages) for fault localization, demonstrating that structured fault signals improve over raw inputs.
\citet{foster2025mutation} deployed LLM-based equivalence detection at scale at Meta, achieving 0.95 precision on mutation testing.
These approaches treat the trace (or patch) as a monolithic input; no prior work has isolated individual trace components to determine their relative contribution to classification, or evaluated whether trace-based classifiers generalize across model families.

\paragraph{Trace Compression and Selection.}
TraceCoder \citep{huang2026tracecoder} inserts diagnostic probes at selected locations rather than recording full traces, improving Pass@1 by 34.4\% for LLM-generated code debugging.
InspectCoder \citep{wang2025inspectcoder} enables LLMs to actively control a debugger for strategic breakpoint placement and runtime state inspection, outperforming baselines by 5--60\%.

\citet{wu2026runtime} used selective variable snapshots in a multi-agent repair debate framework, further validating that targeted trace extraction outperforms full recording.
These methods target repair tasks (generating fixes) rather than classification, and none analyze the information density trade-off between trace completeness and prediction accuracy.

\subsection{Cross-Dataset Validation: DebugBench}
\label{sec:debugbench}

To test whether the component hierarchy generalizes beyond our primary dataset, we evaluate on DebugBench \citep{tian2024debugbench}, a collection of 426 buggy Python code snippets spanning logic, reference, and syntax bugs.
We train separate Qwen-2.5-7B models for each condition using DebugBench's training split and evaluate on its test split.

The results confirm the hierarchy observed on HumanEval+MBPP.
\texttt{exception\_only} achieves 100\% accuracy (426/426; CI [99.14, 100.00]), VOTA achieves 99.77\% (425/426; CI [99.30, 100.00]), and \texttt{no\_trace} achieves 96.71\% (CI [94.80, 98.40]).
The component ranking is preserved: exception events $\geq$ VOTA $>$ \texttt{no\_trace}.
The single VOTA error and 14 \texttt{no\_trace} errors indicate that DebugBench's diverse bug types are equally well-captured by exception signals, consistent with the primary dataset findings.

\subsection{Regex Baseline Comparison}
\label{sec:regex_baseline}

A natural question is whether the \texttt{exception\_only} signal can be captured by simple pattern matching without fine-tuning.
We evaluate five regex baselines that detect error patterns in execution traces: B1 (``ERROR'' string presence, 93.45\%), B2 (``Traceback'' detection, 71.51\%), B3 (any error keyword, 93.45\%), B4 (exception type extraction, 93.61\%), and B5 (format marker ``[FAIL]''/``[PASS]'', 99.33\%).

The strongest \emph{legitimate} regex baseline (B4, matching exception type names) achieves 93.61\%, 6.22pp below SFT \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%; McNemar $p{=}0.041$).
B5 achieves 99.33\% but exploits a format artifact: the ``[FAIL]''/``[PASS]'' markers are inserted by our trace preprocessing pipeline, not by the Python runtime, so its accuracy reflects format leakage rather than genuine trace comprehension.
The SFT advantage over legitimate regex baselines confirms that the fine-tuned model captures exception semantics beyond simple string matching---specifically, the model learns to interpret exception context (type, message, location) jointly, whereas regex baselines treat each pattern independently.
EXPEOF

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{Why Exception Events Dominate}

Verdict prediction is fundamentally a fault detection task: the model must determine whether execution deviated from expected behavior.
Exception events are the most explicit signal of such deviation---structured diagnostic moments that encode the nature and location of a fault.
Unlike loop compressions or assertion-point values, which require the model to integrate information across multiple trace elements, exception events provide a self-contained verdict cue.
This explains why \texttt{exception\_only} matches or exceeds VOTA: adding non-exception trace components dilutes the model's attention on the diagnostic signal rather than providing complementary information.

We acknowledge that exception-based verdict prediction is, at its core, fault indicator presence detection: the model learns to map the presence or absence of a structured error message to a binary label, which is close to trivially solvable for any instruction-tuned LLM.
The Tier~1 accuracy of ${\geq}$99.8\% is therefore unsurprising in isolation.
The contribution of this finding lies not in demonstrating that a strong signal yields high accuracy, but in two less obvious results: (a)~adding more trace information actively \emph{hurts} performance (VOTA $<$ \texttt{exception\_only}, Table~\ref{tab:ablation}), quantifying an information density dilution effect that has not been previously measured; and (b)~this dilution is confounded by tokenizer-driven trace truncation on DeepSeek: the DeepSeek tokenizer produces longer sequences than Qwen for identical inputs, causing the majority of VOTA training samples to exceed the context window (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}); the verdict label is preserved, but the trace content is truncated, depriving the model of diagnostic information and contributing to the collapse of DeepSeek VOTA fail recall to 45.43\% (Table~\ref{tab:per_class}) while Qwen maintains 100\%.

The component ablation (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}) reveals a two-tier diagnostic hierarchy: Tier~1 signals (exception events, assertion points) each achieve ${\geq}$99.8\% individually, while Tier~2 signals (loop compression) reach only 85.6\%.
Combining tiers in VOTA does not improve over the best Tier~1 signal, suggesting a practical design principle: invest extraction effort in preserving high-specificity diagnostic events and discard lower-tier runtime details.
Further analyses of training dynamics, error patterns, and context length sensitivity are reported in Appendix~\ref{sec:training_dynamics_appendix}--\ref{sec:context_length_appendix}.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
Our study has several limitations.
First, all experiments use a single benchmark suite (591 problems from HumanEval and MBPP-sanitized); although DebugBench cross-dataset validation confirms the component hierarchy (\S\ref{sec:debugbench}), generalization to other programming languages---whose exception semantics differ from Python's (e.g., Go's panic/recover, Rust's Result types)---remains untested.
Second, we evaluate only two models at the ${\sim}$7B parameter scale; the relationship between model size and trace signal utility is unexplored.
Third, DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} exhibits seed-dependent variance: 2/3 seeds achieve 99.33\% while seed 123 yields 91.09\% ($\sigma{=}4.76$pp, $n{=}3$), attributable to LoRA initialization sensitivity (fail recall = 70.5\% for the outlier vs.\ 100\% for others); Qwen shows zero variance across seeds.
Fourth, all experiments use LoRA fine-tuning; whether full fine-tuning would eliminate seed sensitivity or alter the relative ranking of trace conditions is unknown.
Fifth, training and test data originate from the same benchmark suite (different problems), potentially inflating accuracy estimates relative to out-of-distribution deployment.
Finally, the candidate solutions were generated by Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, which also serves as one evaluation model; while this does not affect verdict prediction (classifying a \emph{given} solution), the resulting class balance depends on the generator's coding ability.

\paragraph{Future Work.}
Several directions merit investigation: (1)~extending the component hierarchy analysis to additional languages (Java, C++, Rust) where exception and error-handling semantics differ substantially; (2)~scaling to larger models (13B, 70B) to test whether the Tier~1/Tier~2 boundary shifts with model capacity; (3)~evaluating on more diverse benchmarks including LiveCodeBench and real-world CI/CD failure logs; and (4)~deploying exception-based verdict prediction in production test pipelines to measure practical throughput and latency gains over full-trace approaches.
DISCEOF

\section{Simplicity as Relative Robustness}
\label{sec:simplicity_appendix}

The cross-model gap pattern (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) suggests a design principle: \emph{trace representations should match the model capability floor, not the ceiling.}
Exception events are consistently the most effective component on both models, and their structural simplicity---a fixed-format error message---ensures that the relative advantage over richer representations holds across all seeds.
Two of three DeepSeek seeds match Qwen-level accuracy (99.33\%); the outlier (seed 123, 91.09\%) is attributable to LoRA initialization landing in a suboptimal basin (fail recall = 70.5\%), not to a failure of the exception signal itself---even this outlier outperforms VOTA (84.45\%) by 6.64pp.
The VOTA cross-model gap is confounded by two factors: (1)~tokenizer efficiency---the DeepSeek tokenizer averages 2{,}626 tokens per VOTA sample versus Qwen's 1{,}929, causing 91.7\% of training samples to exceed the 2{,}048-token context window, truncating trace content while preserving the verdict label---and (2)~base model capability differences, consistent with findings that SFT generalization depends on pretrain quality \citep{yang2024generalization}.
The two factors cannot be disentangled in the current experimental design; a controlled study with matched tokenizer efficiency would be needed to isolate the model capability effect.

\section{Training Dynamics and Loss Decoupling}
\label{sec:training_dynamics_appendix}

The DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} results reveal two instructive training dynamics.
First, epoch-level analysis shows mild degradation in 2/3 seeds: seed 42 peaks at 99.83\% after epoch~1 but settles at 99.33\% by epoch~3 ($-$0.50pp), seed 123 degrades from 91.43\% to 91.09\% ($-$0.34pp), while seed 456 shows no epoch degradation (99.33\% at both epoch~1 and epoch~3).
Early stopping may yield marginal gains for some seeds, but the epoch effect is small (${\leq}$0.5pp) compared to the seed effect (8.24pp between seeds 42 and 123).

Second, seeds 123 and 456 converge to nearly identical final training losses (0.122 and 0.123 respectively), yet their accuracies differ by 8.24pp (91.09\% vs.\ 99.33\%).
The critical difference lies in fail recall: seeds 42 and 456 achieve 100\%, while seed 123 achieves only 70.5\%---the LoRA initialization in seed 123 fails to learn the exception$\to$fail mapping for a substantial fraction of failing samples, even though the per-token loss appears converged.
This demonstrates that token-level training loss can mask fundamental differences in sample-level classification ability, suggesting a parallel to the eval-loss/accuracy decoupling observed in DeepSeek VOTA (where eval loss rose 65\% from epoch 1 to 3 while accuracy improved by 6.3pp) at the training phase.
The practical recommendation is twofold: (1)~use task-specific metrics (accuracy, fail recall) for checkpoint and seed selection rather than training or evaluation loss, and (2)~for deployment on smaller models, train multiple seeds and select the best, as a single run may not reliably converge to the correct classification boundary.

The contrast with VOTA is instructive: DeepSeek VOTA accuracy monotonically increases from 78.15\% to 84.45\% across epochs, but is consistent with a performance limit associated with the high trace truncation rate (\S\ref{sec:cross_model})---the model progressively extracts signal from samples with intact trace content but cannot fully compensate for the information loss in the truncated majority.
The 84.45\% accuracy reflects a combination of trace information loss and model capability constraints.

\section{Error Analysis}
\label{sec:error_analysis}

Seed robustness testing revealed that the two errors made by \texttt{exception\_only} (accuracy = 99.83\%, 2/1190 incorrect) are \emph{identical across all three seeds} (42, 123, 456).
Both errors are false negatives on samples involving the \texttt{check\_dict\_case} function (sample IDs 901 and 905): the ground truth is \texttt{pass}, but the model predicts \texttt{fail}.
This 100\% error overlap ($\sigma{=}0$) across seeds demonstrates that these are not stochastic training artifacts but \emph{irreducible samples} at the boundary of what exception-based trace signals can resolve.

Manual inspection reveals the root cause: \texttt{check\_dict\_case} (HumanEval/95) uses \texttt{all()} over a generator expression, and Python's \texttt{all()} short-circuits on the first \texttt{True} value, raising \texttt{GeneratorExit} to terminate the generator.
Because \texttt{GeneratorExit} is a \texttt{BaseException} subclass, the tracer records it as seven \texttt{[ERROR] GeneratorExit} lines---even though the function executes correctly and the test passes.
The model observes these spurious error markers and reasonably but incorrectly predicts \texttt{fail}.
This is not a model failure but a \emph{representation ceiling}: the \texttt{exception\_only} format cannot distinguish genuine exceptions from benign \texttt{BaseException} subclasses triggered by Python's iterator protocol.
The 99.83\% accuracy is therefore a deterministic upper bound for this trace representation on this dataset, not an indication of insufficient model capacity.

\section{Sensitivity to Evaluation Context Length}
\label{sec:context_length_appendix}

The three trace conditions exhibit qualitatively different robustness to inference-time context length (\texttt{max\_length}).

\textbf{Full trace is weakly sensitive.}
Evaluating the \texttt{full\_trace} model (trained at \texttt{max\_length}=2{,}048) at \texttt{max\_length}=16{,}384 yields 82.27\%, a +0.51pp gain over the training-time setting (81.76\%; $p{=}0.62$, not significant).
While retaining the complete trace at inference provides slightly more context, the improvement is marginal and within noise---consistent with an accuracy ceiling imposed by trace content quality rather than truncation pattern matching rather than genuine trace comprehension.

\textbf{VOTA is context-dependent.}
VOTA trained at \texttt{max\_length}=2{,}048 (where 91.7\% of samples are truncated) achieves 84.45\% when evaluated at \texttt{max\_length}=16{,}384, recovering performance by restoring the complete structured trace including the terminal ``Answer:'' prompt.
However, the reverse direction fails: evaluating at \texttt{max\_length}=2{,}048 yields only 16.0\%, because content-aware truncation preferentially removes the terminal structured prompt that the model relies on for verdict extraction.
VOTA's accuracy is thus contingent on context length being sufficient to preserve its structured format---a fragility that scales with trace verbosity.

\textbf{Exception-only is inherently robust.}
\texttt{exception\_only} maintains 99.33\% accuracy regardless of evaluation context length.
Because exception events are concise (median 314 tokens), no sample exceeds 2{,}048 tokens; varying \texttt{max\_length} between 2{,}048 and 16{,}384 produces identical inputs and therefore identical predictions.
This robustness is not an engineered property but a natural consequence of signal brevity: there is no truncation to create distribution shift.

These results add an inference-time dimension to the signal quality argument.
Exception-based traces are not only the most accurate at training time (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}) but also the most robust to deployment-time configuration changes---a practical advantage for systems where the evaluation context length may differ from the training setting.
The pattern reinforces a consistent theme: \emph{simpler, shorter signals are more robust because they have fewer failure modes.}

\section{Simplicity as Relative Robustness}

The cross-model gap pattern (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) suggests a design principle: \emph{trace representations should match the model capability floor, not the ceiling.}

The DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} results reveal two instructive training dynamics.

The practical recommendation is twofold: (1)~use task-specific metrics (accuracy, fail recall) for checkpoint and seed selection rather than training or evaluation loss, and (2)~for deployment on smaller models, train multiple seeds and select the best, as a single run may not reliably converge to the correct classification boundary.

The contrast with VOTA is instructive: DeepSeek VOTA accuracy monotonically increases from 78.15\% to 84.45\% across epochs, but is consistent with a performance limit associated with the high trace truncation rate (\S\ref{sec:cross_model})---the model progressively extracts signal from samples with intact trace content but cannot fully compensate for the information loss in the truncated majority.
The 84.45\% accuracy reflects a combination of trace information loss and model capability constraints.

\section{Error Analysis}
\label{sec:error_analysis}

Seed robustness testing revealed that the two errors made by \texttt{exception\_only} (accuracy = 99.83\%, 2/1190 incorrect) are \emph{identical across all three seeds} (42, 123, 456).
Both errors are false negatives on samples involving the \texttt{check\_dict\_case} function (sample IDs 901 and 905): the ground truth is \texttt{pass}, but the model predicts \texttt{fail}.
This 100\% error overlap ($\sigma{=}0$) across seeds demonstrates that these are not stochastic training artifacts but \emph{irreducible samples} at the boundary of what exception-based trace signals can resolve.

Manual inspection reveals the root cause: \texttt{check\_dict\_case} (HumanEval/95) uses \texttt{all()} over a generator expression, and Python's \texttt{all()} short-circuits on the first \texttt{True} value, raising \texttt{GeneratorExit} to terminate the generator.
Because \texttt{GeneratorExit} is a \texttt{BaseException} subclass, the tracer records it as seven \texttt{[ERROR] GeneratorExit} lines---even though the function executes correctly and the test passes.
The model observes these spurious error markers and reasonably but incorrectly predicts \texttt{fail}.
This is not a model failure but a \emph{representation ceiling}: the \texttt{exception\_only} format cannot distinguish genuine exceptions from benign \texttt{BaseException} subclasses triggered by Python's iterator protocol.
The 99.83\% accuracy is therefore a deterministic upper bound for this trace representation on this dataset, not an indication of insufficient model capacity.

\section{Sensitivity to Evaluation Context Length}
\label{sec:context_length_appendix}

The three trace conditions exhibit qualitatively different robustness to inference-time context length (\texttt{max\_length}).

\textbf{Full trace is weakly sensitive.}
Evaluating the \texttt{full\_trace} model (trained at \texttt{max\_length}=2{,}048) at \texttt{max\_length}=16{,}384 yields 82.27\%, a +0.51pp gain over the training-time setting (81.76\%; $p{=}0.62$, not significant).
While retaining the complete trace at inference provides slightly more context, the improvement is marginal and within noise---consistent with an accuracy ceiling imposed by trace content quality rather than truncation.

\textbf{VOTA is context-dependent.}
VOTA trained at \texttt{max\_length}=2{,}048 (where 91.7\% of samples are truncated) achieves 84.45\% when evaluated at \texttt{max\_length}=16{,}384, recovering performance by restoring the complete structured trace including the terminal ``Answer:'' prompt.
However, the reverse direction fails: evaluating at \texttt{max\_length}=2{,}048 yields only 16.0\%, because content-aware truncation preferentially removes the terminal structured prompt that the model relies on for verdict extraction.
VOTA's accuracy is thus contingent on context length being sufficient to preserve its structured format---a fragility that scales with trace verbosity.

\textbf{Exception-only is inherently robust.}
\texttt{exception\_only} maintains 99.33\% accuracy regardless of evaluation context length.
Because exception events are concise (median 314 tokens), no sample exceeds 2{,}048 tokens; varying \texttt{max\_length} between 2{,}048 and 16{,}384 produces identical inputs and therefore identical predictions.
This robustness is not an engineered property but a natural consequence of signal brevity: there is no truncation to create distribution shift.

These results add an inference-time dimension to the signal quality argument.
Exception-based traces are not only the most accurate at training time (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}) but also the most robust to deployment-time configuration changes---a practical advantage for systems where the evaluation context length may differ from the training setting.
The pattern reinforces a consistent theme: \emph{simpler, shorter signals are more robust because they have fewer failure modes.}
